Ahn Sung-mi Subscribe + First deal opens door to potential multibillion-dollar artillery program Hanwha Aerospace’s K9 Mobile Howitzer undergoes a live-fire test at a testing facility operated by the Agency for Defense Development. (Hanwha Aerospace) Hanwha Aerospace said Wednesday it had won a US Army contract to supply prototypes of its K9 self-propelled howitzer, a major breakthrough for the Korean defense industry in the world’s largest defense market. Hanwha Defense USA, the US subsidiary of Hanwha Aerospace, signed an agreement with the US Army on Tuesday to deliver prototypes of K9 Mobile Howitzers for the army’s Mobile Tactical Cannon program, which seeks to replace aging M777 towed howitzers with a highly mobile 155 mm artillery system. Hanwha will deliver six Mobile Tactical Cannon prototypes, with an option for an additional 12 systems. The initial contract is valued at $100.3 million, and could reach up to $262.9 million, according to a separate US Army statement. This award is Hanwha Aerospace’s first major contract with the US Army, according to the company. Hanwha was selected through a competitive process after evaluating artillery systems offered by major global defense companies, including Germany’s Rheinmetall, Britain’s BAE Systems, US’ General Dynamics and Israel’s Elbit Systems. The army plans to acquire up to 18 wheeled self-propelled howitzer systems for rapid prototyping, testing and soldier experimentation over an estimated four-year period, it said. “Soldiers will use these platforms in a series of operational experiments to assess performance, reliability and supportability in realistic combat conditions,” the army said, adding that the results will be used to determine whether the system should move into full-scale deployment. If selected for deployment, the MTC would replace M777 towed howitzers in selected US Army formations, giving those units greater mobility and survivability on modern battlefields. Industry estimates in South Korea put the potential production requirement at around 500 systems, worth about 10 trillion won ($7.14 billion). The US Army has not yet finalized procurement numbers or contract value. Hanwha offered the K9MH, the wheeled artillery system developed from the K9 self-propelled howitzer platform. Unlike the original tracked K9, the K9MH boasts greater strategic and tactical mobility thanks to its wheeled chassis. The latest deal is seen as a payoff from a yearslong push by Hanwha Group Chair Kim Seung-youn and his eldest son, Executive Vice Chair Kim Dong-kwan, to break into the US defense market. Kim Seung-youn has long viewed the defense industry as closely tied to national security, and has urged the group to “secure technology without fear of failure." He has also stressed that Hanwha's defense business should expand beyond the domestic market to be globally competitive. Kim Dong-kwan has continued that strategy, making expansion into the US defense market one of the group's key priorities. Since the early 2020s, the US Army had centered on a tracked self-propelled howitzer equipped with a 58-caliber gun under its Extended Range Cannon Artillery program. But as demand grew for forces and weapons systems that could be deployed rapidly over longer distances, the army began focusing on highly mobile artillery systems, including wheeled platforms. Hanwha said Kim Dong-kwan foresaw that shift and directed the company to prepare for growing US demand for a new generation of highly mobile self-propelled artillery. After spotting a wheeled artillery program in the army’s March 2024 budget proposal, Hanwha Aerospace began developing the K9MH that December to be ready for any potential opportunities. Hanwha has also paired its product development efforts with a localization strategy in the US. In April, Hanwha Defense USA signed a three-year lease for a manufacturing site in Opelika, Alabama, which will serve as the US integration and test facility for K9MH. The move reflects Hanwha’s commitment to “invest in the US artillery system supply chain, enhance America’s combat vehicle industrial base and serve as a long-term artillery modernization partner to the US Army.” The deal also carries symbolic significance for South Korea, which leaned on US military support during the 1950-53 Korean War. “This contract represents a meaningful achievement as the K9 enters the world’s largest defense market,” a Hanwha Aerospace official said. “It also marks a new chapter in the South Korea-US alliance, with a South Korean weapons system contributing to the defense of the US." Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4 , a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine . The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible . But now it has announced its findings. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort." In late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter. However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet" — the network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions. Exactly how and when remains unclear, however. Mixed reactions to Germany's measures For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag , however, the government's response was lacking. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in a DW interview. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said. Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement." However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter has demanded, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia has flatly denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident? On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures. Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target." A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats. Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war." In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said. Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, the Green Party's Nanni fears Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she said, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act." Not at war with Russia From a legal standpoint, too, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under NATO's Article 5 . Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4. But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts have argued that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage. However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Marahrens believes Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens said. He went on to say that "if Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions [to support Ukraine], that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines." AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine The state election on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt is one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state. The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen by many as none of Germany's business, and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine. What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This is why the federal government — composed of the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner. This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia. This article was originally written in German. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Pennsylvania Pennsylvania announces sixth death in measles outbreak as case numbers rise Latest fatality is unvaccinated woman, 39, with ‘underlying conditions’ but CDC still lists only two deaths nationwide Richard Luscombe Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.02 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania ’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100. The most recent fatality was reported in Franklin county on Monday in a statement posted to Facebook by its coroner. The victim was identified as a 39-year-old female who “had several underlying conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment”. The coroner, James Conner, said it was the first measles-related death in the county “for many years” – and that the patient’s recent diagnosis met the definition of the Pennsylvania health department for inclusion. Five other people have died after contracting measles since August in Pennsylvania, which state officials said on Monday had now recorded 1,137 cases and 219 hospitalizations. The outbreak began west of Philadelphia in April, with authorities blaming low vaccination rates. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, continues to list deaths nationally at two amid a dispute between the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy, and Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over the methodology for classifying measles-related fatalities. Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreak Read more The CDC’s website , last updated on Friday, shows 4,080 confirmed measles infections across the US in 42 separate outbreaks, the highest figures in decades, and almost double the number of cases for the whole of 2025. Earlier in October, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared an emergency because of rising case numbers in her state; while Ohio, South Carolina, Texas and Utah have also seen significant increases. A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of the Franklin county fatality – and was “conducting a thorough review of the reported death”. The coroner’s office told the outlet through a spokesperson that the woman’s “primary cause of death was a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles”. The coroner’s office spokesperson said the woman was not vaccinated. Conner’s statement did not identify the woman to protect the privacy of the victim and relatives. “Families deserve the dignity to mourn in private,” that statement said. “We strongly encourage our medical community, first responders, and the public to follow the precautions set forth by” Pennsylvania state guidelines. Those state guidelines recommend two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine, or a combined MMRV vaccine including varicella (chickenpox) protection for children 12 and older. The CDC website recommends the same vaccinations, but Kennedy – a longtime vaccine skeptic – has offered mixed messages. In March 2025, he questioned the effectiveness of the measles vaccine, saying people should be able “to make that choice for themselves ” about whether to take it. And in September, he told anti-vaccine activists at a conference in Washington DC that they had “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House”, a month after telling US families in response to the rise in measles cases nationwide that parents “ should get their children vaccinated ”. The Pennsylvania outbreak has seen 157 new cases over the last week, state figures showed, and one-third of the overall number of infections have come in those 18 or under. Fewer than 1% of cases occurred in those who are fully vaccinated. The first two fatalities, reported in August, were infants, one whose mother had measles during her pregnancy, and the second a six-week-old who also had a rare genetic condition. The other Pennsylvania victims were women aged 40 and 20, and an 18-year-old, all of whom had coexisting health conditions. View image in fullscreen ‘Liverpool was, and still is, a music city’ … the Beatles in 1962. Music Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028 City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building Ben Beaumont-Thomas Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Liverpool is to unveil a new 100,000 sq ft visitor attraction about the Beatles, in plans hailed as “extraordinary” by Paul McCartney , and by Andy Burnham as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain”. Opening in 2028, the project is a huge upgrade for the Beatles Story, a museum which opened in Liverpool’s Royal Albert Dock in 1990. Ownership will now pass to the Beatles company Apple Corps, making the Beatles Story the band’s first official fan experience in their home city. It will also move across the city to the former shopping centre St John’s Market, close to Liverpool’s Lime Street railway station, which has lain unused since closing in 2024. The new site will allow the museum to become four times bigger than its current home. Apple Corps has also announced it will take over and renovate Liverpool’s second-tallest building: St Johns Beacon, a 450ft tower that has also remained unused since 2024, when its viewing gallery closed and its radio station tenants vacated. Neighbouring the redeveloped museum, the tower will become a separate attraction themed around the Beatles’ whimsical and psychedelic animated film Yellow Submarine. View image in fullscreen St Johns Beacon pictured earlier this year. Photograph: Chris Chambers/Alamy The new iteration of the Beatles Story is being billed as a “multi-hour experience” which will recreate settings from the group’s history, from their childhood homes in Liverpool to the city’s Cavern venue and the nightclubs where they cut their teeth in Hamburg, and on to Abbey Road, New York’s Shea Stadium – where Beatlemania provoked such fevered screaming that the band couldn’t hear themselves play – and the building on London’s Savile Row where they played their final rooftop concert in 1969. McCartney said: “I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it’s very exciting to me that the Beatles Story and the Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city. I love Liverpool. It’s part of who I am, it’s part of who the Beatles are. If you’d told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we’d never have believed it.” Ringo Starr also celebrated the plans, saying: “It is great to be part of this – deep down I am still a scouser. “Liverpool was, and still is, a music city. And now we are expanding the Beatles Story … how far out. The beat goes on.” A new charity, the Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, has also been founded. It will receive a portion of every ticket sold, and use that revenue to fund initiatives for local musicians. Andy Burnham praised the Liverpool plans as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain: backing the things our great cities do best and turning that global reputation into jobs, opportunity and growth”. He hailed the charitable arm as helping “the next generation of young artists, wherever they grow up, to believe there is a route from their bedroom, rehearsal room or local venue to the very top of the world.” View image in fullscreen St John’s shopping centre pictured in 2019, part of which will house the new Beatles Story museum. Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/Alamy Liverpool’s mayor Steve Rotheram said: “People already travel halfway around the globe to visit the birthplace of four lads that shook the earth. These plans take that extraordinary pull to another level – creating a world-class destination that will give millions more fans a reason to make the pilgrimage to their spiritual home and experience the city, its music and its culture for themselves.” The project is being helmed by Apple Corps in tandem with Liverpool city council and Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with UK government support. Financial details of the project and its partnerships have not been disclosed. Apple Corps’ chief executive Tom Greene compared the plans with Elvis Presley’s Graceland in Memphis or Dolly Parton’s Dollywood in Tennessee: “A world-class destination for fans to visit in the centre of the city where the story started.” Greene is already overseeing the development of another official Beatles attraction: a renovation of 3 Savile Row where that final rooftop concert took place. The seven-floor museum, due to open in 2027, will allow visitors to access the rooftop and will also recreate the building’s in-house studio where they recorded the Let It Be album, alongside showcases of Apple Corps’ archive and temporary exhibitions. The plans come amid sustained and varied efforts to carry the Beatles’ legacy forward, not least with an ambitious four-film biopic project helmed by director Sam Mendes , telling the stories of each band member. Currently in production, those films will also arrive in 2028, and sets and props will be reused for the recreated environments in the new iteration of the Beatles Story. The band’s Hamburg era is being separately told in Hamburg Days, a forthcoming BBC drama scripted by Succession writer Jamie Carragher, and a reissue programme of the Beatles’ catalogue continues: an expanded version of 1965’s Rubber Soul reached No 2 in the UK charts earlier this month. View image in fullscreen The current iteration of The Beatles Story, in Liverpool’s Albert Dock. Photograph: David A Eastley/Alamy The Beatles are a big tourism draw in Liverpool, with a 2016 study suggesting the band added £82m to the local economy each year. The current iteration of the Beatles Story has helped to drive that success, with exhibits such as George Harrison’s first guitar and John Lennon’s glasses. The museum has won VisitEngland awards for excellence in each of the last two years.
